hints: Focus on what concentrated sulfuric acid does after the first acid-base step, it can act as an oxidising agent toward halide ions.
Remember bromide is a stronger reducing agent than chloride, so the $\text{HBr}$ first formed will reduce sulfur from +6 to +4 to give $\text{SO}_2$.
Think about what the bromide itself is oxidised to, and recall the distinctive colour of that halogen as a vapour.
walkthrough:
**Start with the acid-base reaction**

First, all sodium halides react the same way with concentrated acid. You get the hydrogen halide.

$$\text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HBr}$$
So colourless $\text{HBr}$ gas is made at first.

**Ask if the hydrogen halide can be oxidised**

Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong oxidiser. Chloride cannot reduce it, but bromide can. Bromide is a good enough reducing agent to reduce S(+6) to S(+4).

$$2\text{HBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Link to the observation**

The key product is $\text{Br}_2$. Bromine is a red-brown coloured vapour (with choking fumes of $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ too). That coloured vapour is the classic test to tell bromide apart from chloride.

options.A: Correct. $\text{HBr}$ reduces concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to $\text{SO}_2$ and is itself oxidised to $\text{Br}_2$. Bromine is seen as a dense red-brown coloured vapour.
options.B: Incorrect. Purple refers to iodine, not bromine. $\text{NaI}$ gives purple $\text{I}_2$ vapour (which forms a black solid on cooling). Bromine gives brown, not purple.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ (rotten egg smell) needs a very strong reducing agent. Only iodide is strong enough to reduce S(+6) all the way to S(-2). Bromide only reduces it to $\text{SO}_2$.
options.D: Incorrect. Yellow sulfur is also a product of the iodide reaction, where $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is reduced to S(0). Bromide is not strong enough for that deep reduction, so no sulfur forms.
